title: "CAPM and Beta — Why Market Exposure Matters"
description: "Explain portfolio mathematics with a small numerical example and practical risk limitations."
---

## The question

**Why do investors sometimes demand a different return from two stocks even when both prices swing around a lot?**

A stock that moves strongly with the broad market exposes investors to a type of risk they cannot easily eliminate through diversification. CAPM models that MARKET-LINKED risk with beta.

## Build one relationship

$$
E[R_i]=r_f+\beta_i(E[R_M]-r_f)
$$

**Explain every symbol:** E[R_i] is asset i's expected return required under the CAPM model; r_f is risk-free return; β_i is its sensitivity to the market factor; E[R_M] is the expected return of the market portfolio.

**Substitute concrete numbers:** If the risk-free rate is 2%, the market's expected return 8%, and the stock has β=1.2, required return=2%+1.2×(8%−2%)=2%+7.2%=**9.2%**.

## Why this matters for decisions

The 6-percentage-point market risk premium is multiplied by beta. A beta of 1.2 means that the stock has 20% MORE market covariance per unit of market variance than the market itself under the definition; it does NOT mean the stock always rises exactly 1.2% whenever the market rises 1%.

~~~python
from finance_lab import capm_required_return
print(capm_required_return(.02,1.2,.08)) # .092
~~~

These minimal examples build on the [Finance calculation lab](../examples/index.qmd), where relevant.

## What the model leaves out

CAPM is an equilibrium model with strong assumptions. Beta estimation changes with sample window, leverage, sector and market definition; assets may have other risk factors. Expected returns are not observable facts or guaranteed outcomes.

**Source basis:** Luenberger Investment Science 2e Ch. 7 (market equilibrium, security market line, CAPM).. Text and examples are independently developed.
